claims.text: A simulation approach that explicitly models chemical disorder and anharmonic phonon scattering can predict phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys more accurately than traditional DFT-based or empirical models.
Interatomic-potential simulations can represent chemical disorder in high-entropy alloys.
Combining disorder-averaged interatomic potentials with anharmonic phonon-scattering calculations is an advanced hybrid ab initio method.
The proposed method explicitly samples chemical disorder.
Phonons dominate heat transport in the target alloys at room-to-moderate temperatures.
The target materials are single-phase, chemically disordered, homogeneous solid-solution high-entropy alloys.
Chemical disorder in the lattice enhances phonon scattering.
Enhanced phonon scattering caused by chemical disorder reduces thermal conductivity.
Explicit treatment of chemical disorder and lattice anharmonicity captures reduced phonon mean free paths in high-entropy alloys.
Capturing reduced phonon mean free paths produces thermal-conductivity predictions that align more closely with experiments.
The proposed method will improve predictive accuracy by more than 20% relative to existing models.
The proposed method will enable clear identification of high-entropy alloys with intrinsically low phonon thermal conductivity.
Standard first-principles and simple empirical models often overestimate high-entropy-alloy thermal conductivity.
Conventional models overestimate thermal conductivity because they inadequately capture chemical disorder and anharmonic scattering.
The predictive improvement primarily applies to single-phase, chemically disordered high-entropy alloys in phonon-dominated temperature ranges.
Accuracy may diminish in multiphase or compositionally inhomogeneous systems and where electronic heat transport is significant.
The exact reduction in prediction error is uncertain until comprehensive experimental benchmarking is performed.
TDTR or laser-flash analysis can provide the phonon thermal-conductivity values needed for the benchmark.
The hypothesis is falsified if the new method does not reduce prediction error relative to conventional methods or fails to reproduce the trend across compositions.
